questions.question: What is a stack and what are its core operations?
questions.title: Stack Data Structure Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **stack** is a **LIFO** (Last-In-First-Out) structure with three core operations: **push** (add to top), **pop** (remove from top), and **peek/top** (look at the top without removing), plus **isEmpty**. All are **O(1)**. Think of a stack of plates - you add and remove from the same end. In Java, prefer **`ArrayDeque`** over the legacy `Stack` class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the LIFO principle, the O(1) operations, and the preferred Java class
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending the legacy synchronized Stack class, or forgetting peek vs pop distinction
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use ArrayDeque (not Stack), and name real uses: call stack, undo, DFS, expression parsing

sections.title: The Stack: LIFO and Its Operations
sections.content:
A **stack** follows **LIFO** - the **last** element pushed is the **first** popped. All access happens at one end, the **top**. Like a stack of plates: you put a plate on top and take one off the top.

Core operations, all **O(1)**: **`push(x)`** adds to the top, **`pop()`** removes and returns the top, **`peek()`** returns the top **without** removing it, and **`isEmpty()`** checks if it's empty. In Java, use **`Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()`** - the legacy `Stack` class extends `Vector` and is synchronized (slower, and exposes index access that breaks the abstraction). Stacks power the **call stack**, **undo/redo**, **DFS**, **backtracking**, and **expression evaluation**.

sections.title: Stack Operations with ArrayDeque
sections.content:
```java
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();   // preferred over Stack
stack.push(10);     // top -> 10
stack.push(20);     // top -> 20, then 10
stack.push(30);     // top -> 30, 20, 10

System.out.println(stack.peek());  // 30 (look, don't remove)
System.out.println(stack.pop());   // 30 (remove and return)
System.out.println(stack.pop());   // 20
System.out.println(stack.isEmpty());  // false (10 remains)
```
`push`/`pop`/`peek` all operate on the same end (top) in O(1).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using legacy `Stack`**: it extends `Vector`, is synchronized (slower), and leaks index access - use `ArrayDeque`.
- **peek vs pop**: `peek` only looks; `pop` removes. Mixing them up corrupts logic.
- **pop on empty**: `ArrayDeque.pop()` throws `NoSuchElementException` - check `isEmpty()` first.
- **Confusing with queue**: stack is LIFO; queue is FIFO.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Stack = **LIFO**; all access at the **top**.
- **push, pop, peek, isEmpty** - all **O(1)**.
- Prefer **`ArrayDeque`** over the legacy `Stack` class.
- `peek` looks; `pop` removes.
- Powers call stack, undo, **DFS/backtracking**, expression parsing.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A stack is a last-in, first-out data structure, LIFO for short. That means the most recently added element is the first one to come out, and all the action happens at one end, which we call the top. The classic mental model is a stack of plates: you place a new plate on top, and when you take one, you take it off the top, so the last plate you added is the first you remove. The core operations are push, which adds an element to the top; pop, which removes and returns the top element; peek, sometimes called top, which lets you look at the top element without removing it; and isEmpty, which tells you whether the stack has any elements. All of these are O of one, constant time, because they only touch the top. In Java, the thing I'd emphasize is which class to use. There's a legacy Stack class, but I avoid it, because it extends Vector, it's synchronized so it's slower, and it exposes index-based access that breaks the clean stack abstraction. Instead I use a Deque, specifically ArrayDeque, with push, pop, and peek. A couple of things to be careful about: peek only looks while pop removes, so mixing them up changes behavior, and calling pop on an empty ArrayDeque throws an exception, so I check isEmpty first. Stacks show up everywhere: the program call stack itself, undo and redo features, depth-first search and backtracking, and parsing or evaluating expressions like checking balanced parentheses.

questions.question: What is a queue and how does it differ from a stack?
questions.title: Queue Data Structure Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **queue** is **FIFO** (First-In-First-Out): you **enqueue** at the back and **dequeue** from the front, like a checkout line. A **stack** is **LIFO** (Last-In-First-Out), adding and removing from the same end. Both have **O(1)** core operations; the difference is **which end** you remove from. In Java, use **`ArrayDeque`** for both (as a stack via push/pop, as a queue via offer/poll).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can state FIFO vs LIFO clearly and map each to its operations and use cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up which end items leave from, or recommending LinkedList/Stack over ArrayDeque
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map FIFO->BFS/scheduling and LIFO->DFS/undo, and note ArrayDeque serves both roles

sections.title: Queue (FIFO) vs Stack (LIFO)
sections.content:
Both store elements and have **O(1)** add/remove, but they differ in **which end you remove from**. A **queue** is **FIFO** - the first element added is the first removed. You **enqueue** (add) at the **back** and **dequeue** (remove) from the **front**, like people in a checkout line. A **stack** is **LIFO** - the last element added is the first removed, with add and remove both at the **top**.

This ordering drives their uses: queues model **fair, in-order processing** (BFS, task scheduling, message buffers), while stacks model **most-recent-first** behavior (DFS, undo, call stack, expression parsing). In Java, **`ArrayDeque`** implements both - use `push`/`pop` for stack semantics, `offer`/`poll` for queue semantics.

sections.content:

amber|Queue uses|~in-order/fair|BFS traversal|task scheduling|message buffers
rose|Stack uses|~most recent first|DFS, backtracking|undo/redo|call stack, expressions

sections.content:
| Aspect | Queue | Stack |
|---|---|---|
| Order | FIFO | LIFO |
| Add | enqueue (back) | push (top) |
| Remove | dequeue (front) | pop (top) |
| Remove which | oldest | newest |
| Typical use | BFS, scheduling | DFS, undo, parsing |
| Java class | `ArrayDeque` (offer/poll) | `ArrayDeque` (push/pop) |

sections.title: Queue (FIFO) - oldest comes out first
sections.content:
```java
Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
q.offer(1); q.offer(2); q.offer(3);   // back: ...3
System.out.println(q.poll());  // 1 (oldest first)
System.out.println(q.poll());  // 2
```

sections.title: Stack (LIFO) - newest comes out first
sections.content:
```java
Deque<Integer> s = new ArrayDeque<>();
s.push(1); s.push(2); s.push(3);      // top: 3...
System.out.println(s.pop());   // 3 (newest first)
System.out.println(s.pop());   // 2
```
Same `ArrayDeque` class - the methods you call decide FIFO vs LIFO behavior.

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **Queue (FIFO)**: process items in arrival order - **BFS** level-order traversal, task/job scheduling, producer-consumer buffers, rate limiting.
- **Stack (LIFO)**: process most-recent first - **DFS**, backtracking, undo/redo, matching parentheses, evaluating expressions, the call stack.
- Need both ends? A **Deque** (double-ended queue) supports add/remove at front and back.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Queue = FIFO** (remove oldest); **Stack = LIFO** (remove newest).
- Queue: enqueue back / dequeue front; Stack: push/pop at top.
- Both **O(1)** core ops.
- Queue -> **BFS/scheduling**; Stack -> **DFS/undo/parsing**.
- Java: **`ArrayDeque`** serves both; avoid legacy `Stack`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Both a queue and a stack store elements with O of one add and remove, and the fundamental difference is which end you remove from. A queue is first in, first out, FIFO. You add at the back, called enqueue, and you remove from the front, called dequeue, so the element that's been waiting longest comes out first. The everyday analogy is a checkout line: first come, first served. A stack is last in, first out, LIFO. You add and remove from the same end, the top, so the most recently added element comes out first, like a stack of plates. That ordering difference is what determines where you use each. A queue models fair, in-order processing, so it's the natural structure for breadth-first search, where you process nodes level by level, and for task scheduling, message buffers, and producer-consumer pipelines. A stack models most-recent-first behavior, so it's used for depth-first search and backtracking, for undo and redo, for the program's call stack, and for parsing expressions like matching parentheses. In Java, the practical advice is to use ArrayDeque for both. If I call push and pop I get stack semantics, and if I call offer and poll I get queue semantics. I avoid the legacy Stack class because it's synchronized and slower, and I avoid LinkedList as a queue because ArrayDeque is faster and cleaner. And if I need to add and remove at both ends, a Deque, a double-ended queue, gives me that flexibility.

questions.question: How do you check for balanced parentheses using a stack?
questions.title: Balanced Parentheses Stack Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use a **stack**. Scan the string: **push** every opening bracket; on a **closing** bracket, **pop** and check it matches the expected opener - if it doesn't match (or the stack is empty), the string is invalid. At the end, the stack must be **empty**. **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space. The stack naturally enforces the **innermost-must-close-first** (LIFO) rule.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you map nested brackets to a stack and handle empty-stack and leftover-stack cases
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to check the stack is empty at the end, or popping an empty stack on a closing bracket
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a map of close->open and check both the mismatch and the empty-at-end conditions

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Stack's **LIFO** matches the innermost-closes-first rule.
- **Push** openers; on a closer, **pop** and check the match.
- Invalid if stack empty on a closer, mismatch, or **non-empty at end**.
- Use a **close->open map** for clean type checking.
- **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: This is a textbook stack problem, and the reason a stack fits so naturally is that brackets have to close in the reverse order they were opened, the most recently opened bracket must close first, which is exactly the last-in, first-out behavior of a stack. So I scan the string left to right. Every time I see an opening bracket, a round, square, or curly one, I push it onto the stack. Every time I see a closing bracket, I need to confirm that the most recent unclosed opener matches it. So I check the top of the stack, and there are two ways it can fail right there: if the stack is empty when I hit a closing bracket, there's nothing for it to match, so it's invalid, and if the bracket I pop isn't the correct matching opener, the types or order are wrong, so it's also invalid. If it matches, I pop it and continue. After I've scanned the entire string, there's one final check that freshers often forget: the stack must be empty. If there are leftover opening brackets on the stack, like in a string of three open parentheses, those were never closed, so the string is invalid. The whole thing is O of n time and O of n space. I usually keep a small map from each closing bracket to its matching opener to make the comparison clean. And I'd note that simply counting brackets only works if there's a single bracket type; with mixed types you genuinely need the stack to track order.

sections.title: The stack stores unmatched opening brackets
sections.content:
Scan the expression from left to right. Push every opening bracket. For a closing bracket, the most recently opened bracket must be on top of the stack and must be its matching type.

**Worked example: `{[()]}`**

Push `{`, `[`, and `(`. The next character is `)`, which matches `(`, so pop it. Then `]` matches `[` and `}` matches `{`. The scan ends with an empty stack, so the expression is balanced.

There are two immediate failure cases. A closing bracket with an empty stack has no opener—for example `]abc`. A closing bracket that does not match the top opener breaks nesting—for example `([)]`: when `)` arrives, `[` is on top. After the scan, a non-empty stack means some opening brackets were never closed, as in `(()`.

Ignoring non-bracket characters is fine when the input is an expression, but the accepted character rules should be clear. A mapping from closing to opening symbols keeps the comparison readable.

Each bracket is pushed and popped at most once, so time is O(n). In the worst case, all characters are opening brackets, so the stack uses O(n) space. `ArrayDeque<Character>` is preferred to the legacy `Stack` class for this LIFO work in modern Java.

sections.title: Bracket Matching Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[stack empty] --> B{next char?}
    B -- opening --> C[push it]
    C --> B
    B -- closing --> D{stack empty?}
    D -- yes --> X[invalid]
    D -- no --> E[pop top]
    E --> F{matches opener?}
    F -- no --> X
    F -- yes --> B
    B -- end --> G{stack empty?}
    G -- yes --> Y[valid]
    G -- no --> X
```

sections.title: Valid Parentheses with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No empty-at-end check**: `"((("` leaves openers on the stack - must verify it's empty.
- **Popping an empty stack**: a closer with an empty stack (`")"`) is invalid - check first.
- **Ignoring bracket type**: `"[)"` has equal counts but wrong types - compare the actual opener.
- **Counting only**: a counter works for one bracket type but fails for mixed types/order.

sections.title: A counter is not enough for mixed bracket types
sections.content: A simple counter can validate one bracket type such as only `(` and `)`, but it cannot distinguish the nesting in `([)]`. A stack remembers the exact most recent opener, so it handles `()`, `[]`, and `{}` together in O(n) time. The O(n) worst-case stack space is the cost of preserving nesting information; `ArrayDeque` is the normal Java implementation.

questions.question: What is ArrayDeque and why is it preferred over Stack and LinkedList for stack/queue operations in Java?
questions.title: ArrayDeque vs Stack vs LinkedList Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`ArrayDeque`** is a resizable-array double-ended queue that's the **preferred** choice for both stacks and queues in Java. It beats the legacy **`Stack`** (which extends `Vector` and is **synchronized**/slow) and **`LinkedList`** (which has poor cache locality and per-node memory overhead). `ArrayDeque` gives **O(1)** add/remove at both ends with contiguous-array speed - but it's **not thread-safe** and **disallows null**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know why ArrayDeque is preferred over Stack and LinkedList for stack/queue use
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to Stack or LinkedList out of habit, or assuming ArrayDeque is thread-safe
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Cite Stack's synchronization/Vector inheritance and LinkedList's cache/memory cost as the reasons

sections.title: Why ArrayDeque Wins for Stacks and Queues
sections.content:
**`ArrayDeque`** is a **double-ended queue** backed by a **resizable circular array**. It supports **O(1)** insertion and removal at **both ends**, making it ideal as either a stack (`push`/`pop`) or a queue (`offer`/`poll`).

Why prefer it? The legacy **`Stack`** extends **`Vector`**, so it's **synchronized** (locking overhead even single-threaded) and leaks index-based access that breaks the stack abstraction. **`LinkedList`** can act as a deque but scatters nodes across memory (**poor cache locality**) and adds a per-node pointer overhead. `ArrayDeque`'s contiguous array is **faster** and lighter. The tradeoffs: it's **not thread-safe** (use `ConcurrentLinkedDeque` if needed) and it **does not allow null** elements (null is reserved as an absent-value sentinel).

sections.content:

rose|Legacy Stack|~extends Vector|synchronized = slow|leaks index access|avoid in new code
amber|LinkedList|~node per element|poor cache locality|extra pointer memory|slower in practice
blue|Caveats|~know the limits|not thread-safe|no null elements|use Concurrent variant if needed

sections.title: ArrayDeque as Stack and Queue
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Defaulting to `Stack`**: synchronized + `Vector` inheritance; use `ArrayDeque`.
- **`LinkedList` as a queue**: works but slower (cache misses, pointer overhead).
- **Assuming thread safety**: `ArrayDeque` is **not** synchronized; use `ConcurrentLinkedDeque`/`LinkedBlockingDeque`.
- **Storing null**: `ArrayDeque` rejects null - it's used internally as a sentinel.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`ArrayDeque`** = resizable-array deque; **O(1)** at both ends.
- Preferred over `Stack` (**synchronized**, `Vector`-based) and `LinkedList` (**cache-poor**).
- Serves as both **stack** (push/pop) and **queue** (offer/poll).
- **Not thread-safe**; **no null** elements.
- Faster in practice due to contiguous memory.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: ArrayDeque is a double-ended queue backed by a resizable circular array, and it's the class I reach for whenever I need a stack or a queue in Java. It gives O of one insertion and removal at both ends, so it works as a stack using push and pop, or as a queue using offer and poll. The reason it's preferred comes down to comparing it against the two classes people often use out of habit. The legacy Stack class extends Vector, which means it's synchronized, so you pay locking overhead on every operation even in single-threaded code, and it inherits index-based access from Vector that breaks the clean stack abstraction. LinkedList can also act as a deque, but it allocates a separate node for every element, which scatters data across memory and gives poor cache locality, plus each node carries pointer overhead. ArrayDeque, with its contiguous backing array, is faster in practice and uses less memory. There are two important caveats. First, ArrayDeque is not thread-safe, so if I need concurrent access I'd use something like ConcurrentLinkedDeque or LinkedBlockingDeque instead. Second, ArrayDeque does not allow null elements; it throws a NullPointerException if you try to add null, because it uses null internally as a sentinel to mean absent. So the short version is: use ArrayDeque for stacks and queues, avoid the synchronized legacy Stack and the cache-unfriendly LinkedList, and remember it's neither thread-safe nor null-friendly.

questions.question: What are the real-world use cases of Stack and Queue in software engineering?
questions.title: Stack and Queue Real-World Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **Stacks** (LIFO) power the **call stack**, **undo/redo**, **DFS/backtracking**, **expression evaluation**, and the browser **back button**. **Queues** (FIFO) power **task/job scheduling**, **BFS**, **message queues** (Kafka/RabbitMQ buffering), **printer spoolers**, and **rate limiting**. The rule of thumb: use a stack when you need **most-recent-first**, a queue when you need **fair, in-order** processing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can connect LIFO/FIFO to concrete real systems, not just definitions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing only academic uses (parentheses) and missing real backend systems (message queues, scheduling)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map call stack/undo to LIFO and message queues/scheduling to FIFO with a backend angle

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Stack/LIFO**: call stack, undo/redo, back button, DFS, parsing.
- **Queue/FIFO**: scheduling, BFS, message brokers, spoolers, rate limiting.
- Backend **message queues** decouple producers from consumers.
- Choose by order: **recent-first** vs **fair/in-order**.
- **Deque** covers both-ends needs (sliding window).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The way I decide between a stack and a queue in the real world is by asking which item I want to handle next: the most recently added one, or the one that's been waiting longest. Stacks, being last-in first-out, model reversal and nesting. The most fundamental example is the JVM's own call stack: when methods call other methods, they return in reverse order, which is a stack. Editors use a stack for undo and redo, because you undo the most recent action first. The browser back button is a stack of visited pages. Depth-first search and backtracking use a stack, whether explicit or via recursion. And parsing expressions or checking balanced brackets uses a stack. Queues, being first-in first-out, model fair, in-order processing. Task and job schedulers run jobs in the order they were submitted. Breadth-first search uses a queue to process nodes level by level. In backend systems specifically, message brokers like Kafka and RabbitMQ are essentially queues that buffer work between producers and consumers, which decouples them so a sudden spike of requests doesn't overwhelm a downstream service. Printer spoolers, request buffers, and rate limiters are all queues too. So my one-line rule is: reach for a stack when you need most-recent-first or have to unwind recent actions, and reach for a queue when you need fair, in-order handling or want to decouple producers from consumers. And if I need to add or remove from both ends, like in a sliding-window problem, I use a deque.

sections.title: Ordering decides between a stack and a queue
sections.content:
A stack uses last-in, first-out order, so it fits work whose newest unfinished item should be handled first. A queue uses first-in, first-out order, so it fits work that should be handled in arrival order.

**Stack examples**

- Function calls: the newest call must return before its caller continues.
- Undo: the most recent edit is the first one removed.
- Depth-first search: newly discovered neighbors are explored before older branches.
- Expression parsing: operators and brackets wait until their matching point is reached.

**Queue examples**

- Print jobs and request processing: older accepted work normally runs first.
- Breadth-first search: nodes discovered at one distance are processed before the next distance.
- Buffers: producers append work while consumers take the oldest available item.
- Level-order tree traversal: parents are removed before their children.

The choice is about required order, not about which structure is generally faster. Both can provide O(1) insertion and removal at their working ends. In Java, `ArrayDeque` supports `push/pop` for stack use and `offer/poll` for queue use. A priority queue is different: it removes by priority rather than arrival time. Threaded producer-consumer code also needs a concurrent or blocking queue rather than an ordinary `ArrayDeque`.

sections.content:
rose|Stack LIFO|~most recent first|JVM call stack|undo/redo, back button|DFS, expression parsing
blue|Queue FIFO|~oldest first|task scheduling|BFS traversal|printer spooler
emerald|Backend queues|~decouple work|Kafka, RabbitMQ|producer-consumer buffer|smooth traffic spikes
amber|Pick by need|~order requirement|recent-first -> stack|fair/in-order -> queue|both O(1)

sections.title: Undo (Stack) and Job Buffer (Queue)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **Stack**: undo/redo, navigation history, DFS/backtracking, syntax/expression parsing, anything where you must reverse or unwind recent actions.
- **Queue**: job/task scheduling, BFS, request/message buffering (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS), printer/print spool, rate limiting and producer-consumer decoupling.
- **Deque**: sliding-window problems and work-stealing schedulers that need both ends.

sections.title: The required removal order is the deciding rule
sections.content: Use a stack when the newest item must leave first and a queue when the oldest must leave first. Do not force either structure onto priority-based work; a `PriorityQueue` removes by priority, not arrival time. In multi-threaded producer-consumer code, an ordinary `ArrayDeque` is not safe by itself, so choose a concurrent or blocking queue that also expresses waiting and capacity rules.

questions.question: How do you implement a stack using two queues?
questions.title: Stack Using Two Queues Java
questions.direct_answer: Implement a stack (LIFO) using two queues (FIFO). The clean **push-costly** approach: on **push**, enqueue the new element into the empty `q2`, then **move everything from `q1` into `q2`**, and swap names - so the newest element is always at the front. **push is O(n)**, **pop/top are O(1)**. (You could instead make pop costly and push O(1).)

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can simulate LIFO using FIFO structures and analyze the cost shift
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not committing to which operation is O(n), or losing element order during the transfer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the tradeoff: make push O(n) for O(1) pop, or the reverse, and that a single queue can also work

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Two FIFO queues simulate one LIFO stack.
- **Push-costly**: new element first, move rest behind, swap -> O(n) push, O(1) pop.
- Or **pop-costly**: O(1) push, O(n) pop.
- Always **swap** the queue references after the transfer.
- A **single queue** + rotation also works.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The challenge here is that a queue is first-in first-out, but a stack is last-in first-out, so I have to arrange for the most recently pushed element to be the first one out. The clean approach uses two queues, and I'll make push the expensive operation so that pop and top are constant time. I keep a main queue, q1, and a helper, q2. When I push a new element, I first enqueue it into the empty helper queue q2. Then I move every element from q1 over to q2, one by one, so they line up behind the new element. Now q2 has the newest element at its front, followed by all the older ones in the right order. Finally I swap the references so q1 becomes the queue with the newest element at the front. Because of that arrangement, popping or peeking is just taking from the front of q1, which is O of one. The whole cost lives in push, which is O of n because I move every existing element each time. I'd explicitly state that this is a tradeoff: I chose to make push O of n and pop O of one, but you can flip it and make push O of one and pop O of n by doing the transfer at pop time instead. The detail that's easy to get wrong is the ordering during the transfer, I have to enqueue the new element first and then move the old queue behind it, and I must remember to swap the two queue references at the end. I'd also mention you can actually do this with a single queue by rotating it after each push. For example, after `push(1)`, the main queue is `[1]`. For `push(2)`, put `2` in the helper, move `1` behind it, and swap: the main queue is `[2, 1]`, so `pop()` correctly returns `2`.

sections.title: Move FIFO items to expose the newest value
sections.content:
A queue exposes its oldest element, while a stack must expose its newest. Two queues can reverse which item reaches the front by moving existing elements around a newly pushed value.

**Push-costly worked example**

After `push(1)`, the main queue is `[1]`. To `push(2)`, add 2 to the empty helper queue, move 1 behind it, then swap the queue references. The main queue becomes `[2, 1]`. Repeating this for 3 produces `[3, 2, 1]`, so `pop()` removes 3 immediately.

This version makes `push` O(n), while `pop` and `top` are O(1). A second valid design leaves pushes as normal O(1) queue additions and, during `pop`, moves all but the last element into the helper. That makes `pop` O(n). State which operation is costly; mixing the two designs is a common source of errors.

At all times, only one queue should hold the complete stack order after an operation. Empty checks must happen before `pop` or `top`, according to the chosen API contract.

The structure stores n items across the queues, so it uses O(n) space. The exercise demonstrates adapting one access rule to another; in real Java code, `ArrayDeque` is the direct stack implementation.

sections.title: Push-Costly Stack with Two Queues
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[push x] --> B[q2.offer x] B --> C[move all q1 -> q2
in order] C --> D[swap q1 and q2] D --> E[q1 front = newest] E --> F[pop / top = q1 front
O(1)] ```

sections.title: Stack Using Two Queues (Dry Run)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Undecided cost**: pick a design - push-costly (O(n) push, O(1) pop) or pop-costly.
- **Order lost in transfer**: enqueue the new element first, then move the old queue behind it.
- **Forgetting the swap**: without swapping, `q1`/`q2` roles drift and ordering breaks.
- **Using legacy classes**: use `ArrayDeque` as the underlying queue.

sections.title: Choose which operation pays O(n)
sections.content: A push-costly design rearranges the queues during every push, making `top` and `pop` O(1). A pop-costly design appends pushes in O(1) and moves items only when the newest value is requested, making `pop` O(n). The total storage stays O(n). Pick based on the workload and keep one invariant throughout the implementation rather than mixing the two designs.

questions.question: How do you use a stack to evaluate a mathematical expression?
questions.title: Stack Evaluate Expression Java
questions.direct_answer: Use a **stack**. For **postfix (RPN)**: scan tokens, **push numbers**, and on an **operator** pop the **top two** operands, apply it, and push the result; the final stack value is the answer - **O(n)**. For **infix**, either convert to postfix first (shunting-yard) or use **two stacks** (operands + operators) honoring **operator precedence**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can evaluate postfix with one stack and know infix needs precedence handling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Popping operands in the wrong order for non-commutative ops (subtraction/division), or ignoring precedence in infix
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note operand order matters (second pop is the left operand) and mention shunting-yard for infix

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Postfix**: push operands, on operator pop two, apply, push result.
- **Second pop = left operand** (matters for `-` and `/`).
- Final stack value is the answer - **O(n)**.
- **Infix** needs **precedence**: shunting-yard or two stacks.
- Stack naturally tracks pending operands.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A stack is the natural tool for evaluating expressions. The easiest case is postfix notation, also called Reverse Polish Notation, because it has no parentheses and no precedence rules to worry about. I scan the tokens left to right. Whenever I see a number, I push it onto the stack. Whenever I see an operator, I pop the top two values off the stack, apply the operator to them, and push the result back. When I've processed all the tokens, the single value remaining on the stack is the answer. That's O of n time. The detail I'm careful about is operand order for non-commutative operators like subtraction and division. The first value I pop is actually the right operand, and the second value I pop is the left operand, because the left one was pushed first and is deeper in the stack. So for subtraction I compute the second pop minus the first pop, not the other way around. Getting that backwards is a classic bug. For infix expressions, the normal way we write math like three plus four times two, it's harder because I have to respect operator precedence, multiplication binding tighter than addition. The two standard ways to handle that are to first convert the infix expression to postfix using Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm and then evaluate the postfix, or to use two stacks directly, one for operands and one for operators, applying higher-precedence operators before lower ones. So my answer is: one stack for postfix, and precedence handling via shunting-yard or two stacks for infix.

sections.title: Why postfix removes precedence ambiguity
sections.content:
A postfix expression puts each operator after its operands, so a stack can evaluate it without parentheses or precedence rules. Push numbers as they appear. On an operator, pop the right operand first, then the left operand, apply the operator, and push the result.

**Worked example: `2 3 4 * +`**

Push 2, 3, and 4. `*` pops right 4 and left 3, then pushes 12. `+` pops right 12 and left 2, then pushes 14. At the end, exactly one value remains, so the result is 14.

Operand order matters for subtraction and division. For `8 2 /`, popping gives right 2 and left 8, so the calculation is `8 / 2`, not `2 / 8`.

For an ordinary infix expression such as `2 + 3 * 4`, a second operator stack or a conversion to postfix is needed to handle precedence, associativity, and parentheses. Tokens should be parsed rather than assuming every number has one digit. Invalid input includes too few operands for an operator or more than one value left after all tokens are processed.

Each token is pushed or popped a constant number of times, so postfix evaluation is O(n) time and O(n) stack space in the worst case.

sections.title: Postfix Evaluation Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[stack empty] --> B{next token?}
    B -- number --> C[push number]
    C --> B
    B -- operator --> D[b = pop  right]
    D --> E[a = pop  left]
    E --> F[push a op b]
    F --> B
    B -- end --> Z[answer = pop]
```

sections.title: Evaluate RPN with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Operand order**: for `-`/`/`, the **second** pop is the left operand; swapping gives wrong results.
- **Infix without precedence**: evaluating `3 + 4 * 2` left to right ignores that `*` binds tighter.
- **Empty stack / malformed input**: too few operands means an invalid expression.
- **Integer division/overflow**: be aware of truncation and large intermediate values.

sections.title: Postfix is simple; infix needs operator rules
sections.content: Postfix evaluation needs one value stack because token order already encodes precedence. Infix evaluation requires conversion to postfix or a second operator stack that handles precedence, associativity, and parentheses. The extra parsing logic is justified only when infix input is required. In both forms, tokenization and invalid-expression checks matter more than assuming every operand is a single digit.

questions.question: What is a monotonic stack and what problems does it solve?
questions.title: Monotonic Stack Pattern Java
questions.direct_answer: A **monotonic stack** keeps its elements in **sorted order** (always increasing or always decreasing) by **popping** any element that would break the order before pushing. It solves **next/previous greater (or smaller) element** problems in **O(n)** total - each element is pushed and popped at most once - instead of the O(n^2) brute force. Classic uses: daily temperatures, stock span, largest rectangle in histogram.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the pop-while-violation invariant and the amortized O(n) analysis
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not seeing why it's O(n) (each element pushed/popped once), or storing values when indices are needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the amortized O(n) (each index in/out once) and store indices for distance-based answers

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Keeps a **monotonic** (increasing/decreasing) order by popping violators.
- Solves **next/previous greater/smaller** in **O(n)** (amortized).
- Each element **pushed and popped once**.
- Store **indices** for distance/width answers.
- Classics: **daily temperatures**, stock span, **largest rectangle in histogram**.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A monotonic stack is a stack whose elements are kept in a consistent order, either always increasing or always decreasing. I maintain that order by popping any element that would violate it before I push the new element. And the clever part is that the moment I pop something is exactly when I've discovered a relationship, like the next greater element. The reason this pattern is so valuable is that it solves next-greater, next-smaller, previous-greater, and previous-smaller element problems in O of n total time, whereas the brute force of comparing each element against all the others is O of n squared. The key to seeing why it's linear is the amortized analysis: each element is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped at most once, so even though there's a nested while loop, the total number of pushes and pops across the whole run is bounded by two n, which is O of n. A concrete example is the daily temperatures problem, where for each day I want to know how many days until a warmer temperature. I use a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. For each new day, while the current temperature is warmer than the temperature at the index on top of the stack, I pop that index, and the current day is its next warmer day, so I record the distance as the difference in indices. Then I push the current index. A couple of tips: I store indices rather than values whenever the answer involves a distance or width, and I pick the stack direction based on the question, decreasing for next-greater, increasing for next-smaller. Indices left on the stack at the end simply have no greater element.

sections.title: Each index waits for its next greater value
sections.content:
A monotonic stack stores unresolved candidates in increasing or decreasing order. When a new value breaks that order, it answers the question for one or more stored candidates before they are removed.

**Worked example: daily temperatures `[73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]`**

Store indexes whose warmer day is not known yet. Temperature 74 is warmer than 73, so pop index 0 and record a wait of 1 day. Temperature 75 resolves index 1. Values 71 and 69 remain stacked; when 72 arrives, it resolves 69 after 1 day and 71 after 2 days. Later 76 resolves 72, 75, and any smaller unresolved values.

Indexes are stored instead of only temperatures because the answer needs a distance. The stack is decreasing by temperature from bottom to top; every item on it is still waiting for a greater value to its right.

Although one new value may trigger several pops, each index is pushed once and popped at most once. Total time is therefore O(n), not O(n²), and space is O(n). Changing the comparison changes the problem: a decreasing stack finds next-greater values, while an increasing stack can find next-smaller values. Decide whether equal values should pop based on whether the question asks for strictly greater or greater-or-equal.

sections.title: Next Greater via Monotonic Stack
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[stack of indices
empty] --> B{next i?} B -- yes --> C{stack non-empty AND
nums i > nums stack.top?} C -- yes --> D[j = pop
answer j = i - j] D --> C C -- no --> E[push i] E --> B B -- no --> Z[leftover indices:
no greater element] ```

sections.title: Daily Temperatures with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking it's O(n^2)**: the nested while is **amortized O(n)** - each index enters/leaves once.
- **Storing values not indices**: distance-based answers (days, widths) need indices.
- **Wrong monotonic direction**: next-greater uses a **decreasing** stack; next-smaller uses increasing.
- **Forgetting leftovers**: indices still on the stack have no greater/smaller element (answer 0 / -1).

sections.title: Linear processing for one-direction neighbor queries
sections.content: A nested scan can find the next greater value in O(n²), while a monotonic stack reduces it to O(n) by keeping only unresolved candidates. The O(n) stack is worthwhile when answers depend on the nearest greater or smaller item in one direction. It is not a general replacement for sorting or range-query structures; the comparison direction and equality rule must match the exact question.
